blocks.body:
A triangle has many special points, and they are not independent of each other. The circumcentre, the centroid and the orthocentre always lie on one line, at fixed ratios along it. Nine natural points always lie on one circle of half the circumradius. The distance between the circumcentre and the orthocentre is determined by $R$ and the side lengths. Recognising such a configuration is often most of an olympiad solution.

This lesson defines the classical centres, proves Ceva's and Menelaus's theorems, and proves the Euler line, the nine-point circle and $OH^2 = 9R^2 - (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)$ with vectors. Notation is as in [[euclid-basics]]; in addition $s = \frac{a+b+c}2$ is the semiperimeter and $r$ the inradius.

blocks.title: The four classical centres
blocks.body:
- The centroid $G$ is the common point of the three medians, the segments from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
- The circumcentre $O$ is the common point of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides; it is the centre of the circumcircle, of radius $R$.
- The incentre $I$ is the common point of the internal angle bisectors; it is the centre of the incircle, which touches all three sides and has radius $r$.
- The orthocentre $H$ is the common point of the three altitudes, the lines through each vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.

Each definition claims that three lines pass through one point, and that claim has to be proved.

blocks.title: Why the lines concur
blocks.body:
For $O$ and $I$ the reason is a locus. The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is the set of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$. The point where two perpendicular bisectors meet is equidistant from all three vertices, so it lies on the third. Likewise the internal bisector of angle $A$ consists of the points inside the angle that are equidistant from lines $AB$ and $AC$, and the same argument gives $I$, at a common distance $r$ from all three sides.

Let the incircle touch $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$. The two tangent segments from a point to a circle are equal ([[circles]]), so we may write $x = AE = AF$, $y = BF = BD$, $z = CD = CE$. Then $y + z = a$, $z + x = b$, $x + y = c$, and solving,
$$x = s - a, \qquad y = s - b, \qquad z = s - c.$$
Splitting the triangle into the three triangles $IBC$, $ICA$, $IAB$ with heights $r$ gives $[ABC] = \frac12 r(a + b + c) = rs$. The excircle opposite $A$ touches side $BC$ and the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$; the same splitting, with one triangle subtracted, gives its radius $r_a = [ABC]/(s - a)$.

For $G$ and $H$ the cleanest proofs use Ceva's theorem or vectors, both below.

blocks.title: Ceva's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $D$, $E$, $F$ be points in the interiors of the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. The cevians $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ are concurrent if and only if
$$\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB} = 1.$$

Suppose the cevians meet at $P$, necessarily inside the triangle. Triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$ have the same height from $A$, so $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{[ABD]}{[ADC]}$; for the same reason $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{[PBD]}{[PDC]}$. If $u = kv$ and $u' = kv'$ then $u - u' = k(v - v')$, so subtracting,
$$\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{[ABD] - [PBD]}{[ADC] - [PDC]} = \frac{[ABP]}{[ACP]}.$$
In the same way $\frac{CE}{EA} = \frac{[BCP]}{[BAP]}$ and $\frac{AF}{FB} = \frac{[CAP]}{[CBP]}$. The product of the three right-hand sides is $1$.

Conversely, suppose the product is $1$. The cevians $AD$ and $BE$ meet at a point $P$ inside the triangle; let line $CP$ meet $AB$ at $F'$. By the first part, the product with $F'$ in place of $F$ is also $1$, so $AF'/F'B = AF/FB$. As $X$ moves from $A$ to $B$ along the side, $AX/XB$ increases strictly from $0$ to infinity, so it takes each value only once; hence $F' = F$.

Two quick applications: for the medians all three ratios are $1$, so the medians concur; for the angle bisectors the ratios are $\frac cb$, $\frac ac$, $\frac ba$ by the angle bisector theorem, with product $1$.

blocks.title: Menelaus's theorem
blocks.body:
Let a line that passes through no vertex of triangle $ABC$ meet the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$. Then
$$\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB} = 1.$$
With signed ratios, where $\frac{BD}{DC}$ is positive if $D$ lies between $B$ and $C$ and negative otherwise, the product equals $-1$. Conversely, if points $D$, $E$, $F$ on the three side lines, different from the vertices, satisfy the signed equation, then they are collinear.

Let $\ell$ be the line and $h_A, h_B, h_C > 0$ the distances from the vertices to $\ell$. Since $D$ lies on $\ell$ and on line $BC$, dropping perpendiculars from $B$ and $C$ to $\ell$ gives two similar right triangles with a common vertex $D$, so $\frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{h_B}{h_C}$. Similarly $\frac{CE}{EA} = \frac{h_C}{h_A}$ and $\frac{AF}{FB} = \frac{h_A}{h_B}$, and the product is $1$.

For the sign: $D$ lies between $B$ and $C$ exactly when $B$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of $\ell$. Either all three vertices are on one side of $\ell$, and then no ratio is positive, or one vertex is separated from the other two, and then exactly two ratios are positive. In both cases an odd number of ratios is negative, so the signed product is $-1$.

For the converse, let line $DE$ meet line $AB$ at $F'$. (It does meet it: if $DE \parallel AB$, the intercept theorem gives $\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA} = 1$, which would force $\frac{AF}{FB} = -1$, a value no point achieves.) By the first part the signed product with $F'$ is $-1$, so $F$ and $F'$ have the same signed ratio, and a point of line $AB$ is determined by its signed ratio. So $F = F'$ lies on line $DE$.

blocks.title: Vectors from the circumcentre
blocks.body:
Place the origin at the circumcentre $O$ and write $A$, $B$, $C$ also for the position vectors of the vertices (see [[vectors-plane]]). Then $|A| = |B| = |C| = R$, and dot products encode the sides: from $c^2 = |A - B|^2 = 2R^2 - 2A\cdot B$,
$$A\cdot B = R^2 - \tfrac{c^2}{2}, \qquad B\cdot C = R^2 - \tfrac{a^2}2, \qquad C\cdot A = R^2 - \tfrac{b^2}2.$$
The point $\frac{A + B + C}{3}$ equals $A + \frac23\left(\frac{B+C}2 - A\right)$, so it lies two thirds of the way along the median from $A$, and by symmetry on the other two medians as well. This proves at once that the medians concur, at $G = \frac{A+B+C}{3}$, and that $G$ divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$ from the vertex.

blocks.title: The Euler line
blocks.body:
With the circumcentre $O$ as origin, the orthocentre is $H = A + B + C$. Hence $H = 3G$: the points $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear, $G$ lies between $O$ and $H$, and $OG : GH = 1 : 2$ (all three points coincide when the triangle is equilateral). Moreover
$$OH^2 = 9R^2 - (a^2 + b^2 + c^2).$$

Let $P = A + B + C$. Then
$$(P - A)\cdot(B - C) = (B + C)\cdot(B - C) = |B|^2 - |C|^2 = R^2 - R^2 = 0,$$
so $P - A$ is perpendicular to $BC$ or zero, which means that $P$ lies on the altitude from $A$. By symmetry $P$ lies on all three altitudes. So the altitudes concur, at $H = P = 3G$. If $H \ne O$, the line through $O$ and $H$ contains $G = \frac13 H$, with $OG = \frac13 OH$ and $GH = \frac23 OH$. If $H = O$ then $G = O$ as well, so the circumcentre lies on every median, every median is a perpendicular bisector, and the triangle is equilateral.

For the distance,
$$OH^2 = |A + B + C|^2 = |A|^2 + |B|^2 + |C|^2 + 2(A\cdot B + B\cdot C + C\cdot A) = 3R^2 + 2\Big(3R^2 - \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{2}\Big) = 9R^2 - (a^2 + b^2 + c^2).$$
As a by-product, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \le 9R^2$, with equality only for the equilateral triangle.

blocks.title: The nine-point circle
blocks.body: In every triangle, the midpoints of the three sides, the feet of the three altitudes, and the midpoints of $AH$, $BH$, $CH$ lie on one circle. Its centre $N$ is the midpoint of $OH$, and its radius is $R/2$.

Keep $O$ as the origin, so that $N = \frac{A + B + C}{2}$. The midpoint of $BC$ is $M_a = \frac{B + C}{2}$, and $N - M_a = \frac A2$ has length $\frac R2$. The midpoint of $AH$ is $K_a = \frac{A + (A + B + C)}{2}$, and $K_a - N = \frac A2$, again of length $\frac R2$. By symmetry all six midpoints are at distance $\frac R2$ from $N$. Note also that $N$ is the midpoint of $K_a M_a$, so $K_aM_a$ is a diameter of the circle with centre $N$ and radius $R/2$.

Now let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. If $D$ coincides with $K_a$ or $M_a$, it is on the circle already. Otherwise, $D$ and $M_a$ lie on line $BC$, while $D$ and $K_a$ lie on the altitude from $A$ (which contains both $A$ and $H$), so $\angle K_aDM_a = 90^\circ$. By Thales, $D$ lies on the circle with diameter $K_aM_a$. The same holds for the other two feet.

blocks.title: The 13-14-15 triangle
blocks.body: For the triangle with $a = 14$, $b = 15$, $c = 13$, compute the area, $r$, $R$, the exradius $r_a$, the tangent lengths from the vertices to the incircle, and $OH$.
blocks.solution:
Here $s = 21$, so by Heron's formula $[ABC] = \sqrt{21\cdot 7\cdot 6\cdot 8} = \sqrt{7056} = 84$. Then $r = 84/21 = 4$, $r_a = 84/(s - a) = 84/7 = 12$, and $R = \dfrac{abc}{4[ABC]} = \dfrac{2730}{336} = \dfrac{65}{8}$.

The tangent lengths are $s - a = 7$ from $A$, $s - b = 6$ from $B$ and $s - c = 8$ from $C$.

Finally
$$OH^2 = 9\cdot\frac{4225}{64} - (196 + 225 + 169) = \frac{38025 - 37760}{64} = \frac{265}{64}, \qquad OH = \frac{\sqrt{265}}{8} \approx 2.03.$$
Everything can be confirmed in coordinates with $B = (0,0)$, $C = (14, 0)$, $A = (5, 12)$: then $O = (7, \frac{33}{8})$, $H = (5, \frac{15}{4})$ and $I = (6, 4)$.

Euler's relation $OI^2 = R(R - 2r)$, not proved here, gives $OI^2 = \frac{65}{8}\cdot\frac18 = \frac{65}{64}$, in agreement with the coordinates; it implies $R \ge 2r$.

blocks.title: The Gergonne point
blocks.body: Show that the three lines joining each vertex to the point where the incircle touches the opposite side are concurrent.
blocks.solution:
With the tangent lengths found above, $BD = s - b$, $DC = s - c$, $CE = s - c$, $EA = s - a$, $AF = s - a$, $FB = s - b$. So
$$\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB} = \frac{s-b}{s-c}\cdot\frac{s-c}{s-a}\cdot\frac{s-a}{s-b} = 1,$$
and Ceva's theorem gives concurrence. The common point is called the Gergonne point.

blocks.title: Menelaus in action
blocks.body: In triangle $ABC$, the point $F$ lies on $AB$ with $AF : FB = 1 : 2$ and the point $E$ lies on $AC$ with $AE : EC = 3 : 1$. Line $FE$ meets line $BC$ at $D$. Find $BD : DC$.
blocks.solution: By Menelaus's theorem with unsigned lengths, $\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB} = 1$, so $\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac12 = 1$ and $BD : DC = 6 : 1$. Since $E$ and $F$ are interior points of two sides, the signed ratios $\frac{CE}{EA}$ and $\frac{AF}{FB}$ are positive, and the signed product must be $-1$; so $\frac{BD}{DC}$ is negative and $D$ lies on line $BC$ outside the segment, beyond $C$, with $BD = 6\,DC$.

blocks.title: When is the Euler line parallel to a side?
blocks.body: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle that is not equilateral. Prove that its Euler line is parallel to $BC$ if and only if $\tan B\tan C = 3$.
blocks.solution:
Since the triangle is not equilateral, $O \ne H$ and the Euler line $OH$ is defined. In an acute triangle both $O$ and $H$ lie inside, on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, so $OH \parallel BC$ exactly when $O$ and $H$ are at the same distance from $BC$.

Distance of $O$: with $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, the central angle theorem gives $\angle BOM = A$, so $OM = R\cos A$.

Distance of $H$: let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. In the right triangle $ABD$, $BD = c\cos B$. The altitude from $B$ is perpendicular to $AC$, so it makes the angle $90^\circ - C$ with $BC$, and in the right triangle $BDH$ we get $HD = BD\tan(90^\circ - C) = c\cos B\,\dfrac{\cos C}{\sin C}$. With $c = 2R\sin C$ this is $HD = 2R\cos B\cos C$.

So the condition is $\cos A = 2\cos B\cos C$. Since $\cos A = -\cos(B + C) = \sin B\sin C - \cos B\cos C$, it becomes $\sin B\sin C = 3\cos B\cos C$, that is $\tan B\tan C = 3$, dividing by the positive number $\cos B\cos C$.

The equilateral triangle also has $\tan B\tan C = 3$ but no Euler line. A genuine example: $B = 50^\circ$, $C = \arctan(3/\tan 50^\circ) \approx 68.3^\circ$, $A \approx 61.7^\circ$.

blocks.body:
- Ceva's condition as stated is for points inside the sides. If some of $D$, $E$, $F$ lie on extensions, use signed ratios: then the three lines are concurrent or all parallel exactly when the signed product is $+1$.
- Menelaus's product is $-1$ with signed ratios and $1$ without; mixing the two conventions is the most common error.
- The orthocentre lies outside the triangle when the triangle is obtuse, and at the vertex of the right angle when it is right. Arguments drawn for an acute triangle may need adjusting; the vector proofs above work in all cases.
- The incentre is not on the Euler line in general; it is only when the triangle is isosceles.

The homothety with centre $G$ and ratio $-\frac12$ maps $A$, $B$, $C$ to the midpoints of the opposite sides, $H$ to $O$, and the circumcircle to the nine-point circle; [[geo-transformations]] develops this point of view. Barycentric and complex coordinates make computations like the ones above systematic ([[analytic-geometry]]). Euler's inequality $R \ge 2r$ is a starting point of [[geo-inequalities]], the trigonometric form of Ceva's theorem comes from [[trig]], and many problems combine these centres with power of a point from [[circles]].

1. Use Ceva's theorem to show that the altitudes of an acute triangle are concurrent.
2. Prove that the reflection of $H$ in the line $BC$ lies on the circumcircle.
3. Prove that $AH^2 + BC^2 = 4R^2$. (With $O$ as origin, $H - A = B + C$.)
4. Prove that the excircle opposite $A$ touches $BC$ at a point $D'$ with $BD' = s - c$, and deduce that $D'$ is the reflection of the incircle's point of contact $D$ in the midpoint of $BC$.
